content.topic: DC Motor Back EMF and Speed Regulation
content.hook: Weaken the field flux, and a DC motor actually speeds up!
content.question: A DC shunt motor drives a constant torque load. If the field flux is reduced by fifty percent, what happens to the steady state armature current?
content.answerLine: The steady state armature current doubles.
explanation: Electromagnetic torque developed by any direct current machine is proportional to flux multiplied by armature current.
Because the mechanical load torque remains strictly constant, the electromagnetic torque developed must also stay unchanged.
Halving the magnetic flux demands that armature current doubles to maintain the exact same developed torque.
Initially, lowering the flux weakens the back electromotive force, causing a sudden surge in armature current.
content.funFact: Field weakening is widely used in high-speed electric trains to cruise well above base motor speed!
content.outro: Master your electrical machine equations, and follow along for more engineering exam prep!

script.narration: Electromagnetic torque developed by any direct current machine is proportional to flux multiplied by armature current.
Because the mechanical load torque remains strictly constant, the electromagnetic torque developed must also stay unchanged.
Halving the magnetic flux demands that armature current doubles to maintain the exact same developed torque.
Initially, lowering the flux weakens the back electromotive force, causing a sudden surge in armature current.
This current surge creates accelerating torque, speeding up the rotor until a higher steady speed is reached.
At this elevated rotational speed, back electromotive force recovers enough to stabilize the doubled armature current.
The rotational speed roughly doubles because speed is inversely proportional to the operating field flux.
Armature copper losses rise by a factor of four because losses vary with current squared.
Therefore, field weakening provides higher speed operation but causes significantly greater thermal stress on the armature.
